parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: proportionality of current and potential difference
hints: Hint 1: Think about which two electrical quantities Ohm’s law links for a conductor, and what type of relationship (proportional or inversely proportional) it describes.
Hint 2: Remember that resistance only stays constant if a physical condition of the wire does not change - what condition affects lattice vibrations and resistivity?
parts.proper_answer: Current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature of the conductor remains constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what Ohm’s law is about**
You are thinking about how easy it is to push current $I$ through a metal when you apply a voltage $V$ across it. Ohm’s law says the two go up together in a simple linear way, so $I$ is proportional to $V$.

Step 2: **Add the vital condition**
This simple proportionality only holds if the resistance $R$ does not change. In a metal wire, heating makes ions vibrate more and increases resistance, so you must state that temperature remains constant. That gives the full statement: $I$ proportional to $V$ at constant temperature.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: dependence on length and cross-sectional area
hints: Hint 1: Look at the data given for the wire: resistance $R$, length $L$ and area $A$. Think about how resistivity $\rho$ is a material property that links these three geometric quantities.
Hint 2: Use $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$ rearranged to $$\rho = \frac{RA}{L}$$ and check your units give $\Omega \text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link resistance to material and shape**
Resistance is not just a material property. A long thin wire has more resistance than a short thick one of the same material. This is captured by $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$ where $\rho$ is resistivity, $L$ is length and $A$ is cross-sectional area.

Step 2: **Rearrange and substitute**
You need $\rho$, so rearrange first: $$\rho = \frac{RA}{L}$$ Now put in $R = 18 \ \Omega$, $A = 7.2 \times 10^{-8} \ \text{m}^2$, $L = 0.94 \ \text{m}$: $$\rho = \frac{18 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-8}}{0.94}$$ $$\rho = 1.4 \times 10^{-6} \ \Omega \text{ m}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: p.d. proportional to length for uniform wire
hints: Hint 1: With the switch open, no current can flow in the lower loop with the voltmeter and fixed resistor. Focus only on the top loop: the battery is connected directly across the uniform 18 ohm wire, and the slider is half-way along it.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See what the voltmeter measures with switch open**
An ideal voltmeter draws negligible current. With the switch open, the lower branch carries no current, so there is no p.d. lost in the fixed resistor. The voltmeter is effectively connected between the left-hand end of the wire and the slider S.

Step 2: **Use half the length means half the voltage**
The wire is uniform and S is half-way along. The 6.2 V battery is across the whole wire, so the p.d. across half the length is half the total: $$V = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.2 = 3.1 \ \text{V}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: When the switch closes, what new path for current is added? Think about how the fixed resistor is now connected relative to the left half of the resistance wire.

Hint 2: Think about what adding a parallel branch does to total resistance and hence to total battery current, and then what a larger current through the right-hand part of the wire means for the voltage left for the slider section.
parts.proper_answer: Current in the battery increases. Voltmeter reading decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the new parallel combination**
Closing the switch connects the fixed resistor in parallel with the left half of the resistance wire (the section between the left end and S). Two resistors in parallel always give a smaller resistance than either alone.

Step 2: **Follow through to battery current and voltmeter**
Total circuit resistance falls because the left side resistance has fallen, while the right half is unchanged. With e.m.f. 6.2 V and negligible internal resistance, $$I = \frac{E}{R_{total}}$$ so $I$ from the battery increases. More current now flows through the right-hand half of the wire, so more of the 6.2 V is dropped there and less is left across the left parallel section that the voltmeter measures. Hence voltmeter reading decreases.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
key_concepts: effect of slider position on resistance and p.d.
hints: Hint 1: After closing the switch the voltmeter fell below 3.1 V. To bring it back up to 3.1 V you need to increase the resistance of the wire section in parallel with the fixed resistor - think about which way S must slide to include more wire length.
parts.proper_answer: Mark a cross (x) on the wire to the right of the present position of S, not at the far right-hand end.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Work out which way restores the voltage**
Closing the switch lowered the effective resistance on the left and lowered the voltmeter reading. To raise the reading back to 3.1 V you need a larger resistance between the left end and S. For a uniform wire, resistance is proportional to length, so you need a longer length of wire on the left. That means sliding S to the right of its half-way position, but still leaving some wire on the right so the reading is not the full 6.2 V.

parts.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: current as flow of charge carriers
hints: Hint 1: Current in a wire depends on how many carriers per unit volume there are, how fast they drift, the wire area, and the charge on each carrier. Identify $I$, $A$, $v$, $n$ from the data given.

Hint 2: Rearrange $$I = Anvq$$ to make $q$ the subject and substitute $I = 0.93 \text{ A}$, $A = 7.2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ m}^2$, $n = 9.0 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$, $v = 1.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the drift speed model**
Picture charges drifting through the cross-section $A$ at mean speed $v$. In time $t$ they travel $vt$, so the volume passing is $Avt$ and number of carriers is $nAvt$. Total charge is number times $q$, giving $$I = \frac{\text{charge}}{\text{time}} = Anvq$$

Step 2: **Solve for $q$**
Rearrange: $$q = \frac{I}{Anv}$$ Substitute: $$q = \frac{0.93}{(7.2 \times 10^{-8}) \times (9.0 \times 10^{28}) \times (1.3 \times 10^{-3})}$$ $$q = 1.1 \times 10^{-19} \ \text{C}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Compare your value of about $1.1 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ with the smallest free charge known in nature, the charge on an electron or proton.
parts.proper_answer: Calculated $q$ is less than $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, the elementary charge. Charge is quantised so a carrier cannot have less charge than one electron.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply charge quantisation**
All free charges come in multiples of the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$. Your value $1.1 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ is smaller than $e$. A charge carrier, normally an electron, must carry at least $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ in magnitude, so the recorded combination of $I$, $v$ and $n$ cannot be correct.
